newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada raises rates in surprise move.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada raises rates in surprise move.

text.p: Canada's central bank surprised financial markets on Thursday when it raised its key bank rate for the first time in more than two years, citing the need to strengthen the wobbly Canadian dollar.
Analysts said the hike -- the first since February 1995 -- was likely the first of many and marked the end to a rate-cutting cycle that brought Canadians their lowest interest rates in decades.
The Bank of Canada raised the bank rate by 25 basis points to 3.5 percent. The rate is similar to the U.S. federal funds rate.
The increase immediately achieved the bank's goal of strengthening the dollar, which shot up 1 U.S. cent in heavy trading after the announcement.
The currency traded as high as 72.64 U.S. cents after opening on Thursday at 71.63 U.S. cents. The dollar later settled back to 72.44 U.S. cents.3

"This (currency) move in the light of a 25 basis-point-hike has been incredibly dramatic. We've seen easings, we've seen tightenings, but they're usually not this violent," said a currency trader at one of Canada's largest banks.
Royal Bank of Canada economist John Anania called the rate hike "a mild suprise. I don't think market participants altogether expected the bank to react (to the weak dollar)."
The central bank said in a statement after the move that the hike was designed to "counter excessive easing in monetary conditions and to provide support for the currency."
The Bank of Canada said last month that the need for further easing in monetary conditions had largely disappeared, implying it would like to see the dollar strengthen or rates rise.
But the Canadian dollar depreciated afterward and weakened sharply on Wednesday, forcing the central bank to intervene on financial markets to defend the currency.
Canadian bond and T-bill yields moved higher after the tightening, with many traders expressing surprise that the Bank of Canada responded to the currency weakness.

The Bank of Canada last year cut the bank rate 11 times to its lowest level since December 1961 as it sought to spur the sluggish Canadian economy. Ten of the reductions were independent of rate cuts by the Federal Reserve.
Its previous move was a rate cut of 25 basis points on November 8, 1996.
Technical Data analyst Jeoff Hall said the Bank of Canada would likely hike rates several more times this year as it saw more indications that the economy was strengthening.

"Two weeks or so from now we should see the street revisiting the idea that the bank would raise rates again. Certainly the economic evidence is pointing to the need for less stimulative policy," said Hall.
